cells.tense: You are here with the pen, and the fairness you bring to people is steady.
cells.act: release what is done and keep what serves
cells.ask: In a connection you carry, find the piece that has already run its course — a role kept out of habit, an old argument rehearsed — and set that piece down, keeping everything that still lives.
cells.core:
When you're with someone, you feel the whole situation and still keep it even. That isn't distance. You're taking in what's there, weighing it, and holding what's shared at a size both of you can live with. People can lean on you without feeling handled. It's a real thing and it's working.

The practice on top of it is subtraction. In one connection, find the piece that has already finished — the part you keep tending out of habit — and set it down while keeping the rest. What's alive stays; what's done gets released. Nothing much is lost by it. The living part just gets room to breathe again.
cells.sheetLine: The fairness is holding. Something inside it finished.
cells.verb: to hold what's shared at a fair weight.
cells.place: where two people meet as equals.

cells.tense: You are braced for what someone will need next, and the fairness is outrunning the conversation.
cells.act: hold the weight as a builder holds stone
cells.ask: In a conversation this week, before you sort out what's fair, take the whole weight of it and do nothing with it — say nothing, fix nothing — and then answer.
cells.core:
When this side of you is working well, you can sit in a room where something is uneven and stay level in it. You read who's taking too much and who's coming up short, and your presence alone settles the exchange, because you're holding it at a weight everyone can carry. People leave those conversations lighter and don't quite know why.

What's happening now is that same fairness running ahead of its moment. Who'll take too much, who'll come up short, what you'll need to say — the accounting starts while the person is still mid-sentence, and they can feel a scale on them. A builder doesn't force stone into shape, they hold it. In one conversation, before sorting anything out, hold the whole weight and do nothing with it. Then answer.
cells.sheetLine: The fairness is deciding before the person speaks.
cells.verb: to hold what's shared at a fair weight.

cells.tense: You came through the door of this connection and your hands never joined.
cells.act: write the facts down in order, without feeling words
cells.ask: Put one thing that happened with a person on paper, in sequence, using no feeling words, then ask one plain question of that page before closing it.
cells.core:
Something in how you meet someone has gone faint. You're there in body but not in the exchange, and offers can come toward you without landing. The fairness itself hasn't gone. It's that the part of you that used to lean in isn't showing up. Nothing in the moment tells you what's wrong — it only feels like you've decided something.

You can call it back through thinking. Write out one thing that happened with a person, in sequence, no feeling words. That's the whole discipline. Then ask one plain question of what you wrote and put it down. Small, exact, done once, teaches the rest of you how to arrive.
cells.sheetLine: The fairness is still there. It hasn't entered the exchange.
cells.verb: to hold what's shared at a fair weight.
cells.place: where two people meet as equals.

cells.tense: You are already reading the room and you would call it common courtesy.
cells.act: perceive it with fresh eyes before judging
cells.ask: Take an exchange you have already judged — a tone, a silence, what someone seemed to want — and look at it again before your first read settles it.
cells.core:
Something in you keeps things even among people, and you have no name for it. You catch who's been left out, who's carrying too much, when a word needs to be said. Others settle in your company and couldn't say why. That settling is your reading, running through your hands, and you file it under being civil.

You don't need to claim it to learn from it. Take an exchange you've already judged — someone's tone, their quiet, what they seemed to want — and look at it again before the first read settles it. That is where the reading sharpens, in the second look.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that fairness in feeling is already governed with earned authority here — the record has the signature, but the person may hear it as flattery about their emotional maturity, which is not established. The reader could reasonably say 'my feeling isn't governed at all, it's a mess.' Each ask is one small act of releasing, holding, ordering or listening, useful even if the read is wrong. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is the one about arriving at the heart without having to claim the seat first.
